To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The prostate cancer risk is increased in first-degree relatives (FDR) of prostate cancer (PrCa) patients.
relatives of early-onset prostate cancer patients have an increased risk of prostate cancer and stomach cancers.
the relatives of men with prostate cancer have an increased risk of prostate and stomach cancers, and that these risks are highest among the relatives of patients diagnosed with early-onset disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of the genetic factors predisposing to prostate and other common cancers in the Finnish population, and the elucidation of their biological mechanisms.
the identification and characterization of novel genetic risk factors for prostate cancer, which are relevant to the Finnish population.
the identification and characterization of genetic factors involved in prostate cancer development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic risk of prostate cancer is not confined to early onset cases.
the risk to develop prostate and gastric cancer among relatives of prostate cancer cases is increased.
the heritability of prostate cancer is higher in younger age groups than in older groups, and that there are several genetic risk factors for this disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic risk for prostate cancer in the Finnish population is complex and involves multiple genes, which contribute to the risk of prostate cancer at different ages.
the genetic predisposition to prostate cancer is not restricted to families with an early onset, and the risk of gastric cancer may be increased in the relatives of prostate cancer cases.
hereditary factors play an important role also in the late-onset prostate cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of prostate cancer among relatives of patients diagnosed in Finland is higher than previously recognized.
the risk of developing prostate cancer may not be restricted to the first-degree relatives of young-onset prostate cancer patients, as previously thought.

prostate cancer patients should be informed about the increased risks of prostate cancer among their male relatives, especially those diagnosed at an early or late age of onset, and of gastric cancer among the male relatives diagnosed at an early onset.
